case_name: CASE OF BOGAY AND OTHERS v. UKRAINE

assessment.1. Protected expression and existence of: The applicants were taking part in a notified public demonstration against the use of animals in circus acts, using banners and slogans on an issue of public interest (see paragraphs 5-6). A public protest of this kind is a classic form of political and social expression, attracting strong protection under Article 10 and a narrow margin of appreciation (see nos. 29580/12 and 31349/20). The police intervention went well beyond a minimal security check: all applicants were searched, several were handcuffed, all were removed in police vehicles to a police station for about two to three hours, and administrative-offence proceedings were brought against some of them (see paragraphs 10, 13-17). These measures interrupted the protest shortly after it began and were plainly capable of producing a chilling effect. There was therefore an interference with the applicants’ freedom of expression.

assessment.2. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: There was a domestic legal framework for preventive police measures, including surface inspections where there were sufficient grounds to believe that a person carried prohibited or dangerous items (see paragraphs 29-30). After the second applicant was found with a metal rod concealed in his sleeve and a knife, and after officers reported that other demonstrators discarded metal objects and knives, the police could plausibly rely on public-safety concerns to justify searches (see paragraphs 8, 11-12 and 20). The interference also pursued legitimate aims, namely the prevention of disorder or crime and the protection of the rights and safety of others, given the presence of an opposing group and the rising tension on the scene (see paragraphs 7 and 9). However, the more intrusive measure — transferring all the applicants to the police station and keeping them there for hours — is harder to reconcile with domestic law. No administrative-detention reports were drawn up, although domestic law required them, and the internal police investigation expressly criticised that omission (see paragraphs 14, 21(i), 26-28). Since that station transfer effectively removed the applicants from the demonstration, the central interference with their expression was not shown to have been clearly and properly grounded in law.

assessment.3. Necessity and proportionality: risk f: The authorities were not facing a wholly routine protest. A rival group appeared at the scene, a smoke grenade was lit, tensions rose, and the police discovered a significant number of knives, metal rods, hammers and gas canisters among demonstrators or on the ground near them (see paragraphs 7-12). This materially strengthens the State’s argument that some preventive action was necessary. Under the Court’s case-law, Article 10 does not prevent the authorities from taking firm measures where there is a concrete and imminent risk of violence or serious disorder at a demonstration (see no. 4048/09). In particular, targeted searches and confiscation of weapon-like objects could be justified.

assessment.4. Necessity and proportionality: blanke: Even so, the decisive question is whether the response remained individualized and proportionate. The demonstration had initially been peaceful, the entrance to the circus was unobstructed, and the interference affected all the applicants alike (see paragraphs 6, 10, 12 and 14). The domestic material does not show individualized reasons for removing each applicant from the protest; rather, the police surrounded the whole group and extracted participants one by one (see paragraph 10). Article 10 requires particularly weighty reasons before a public-interest protest is effectively shut down. Strasbourg case-law stresses that authorities must distinguish between persons who create a genuine risk and those who remain peaceful, instead of treating all participants as suspects (see nos. 29580/12 and 1162/22). Here, the discovery of dangerous items could justify action against the persons concerned, but it did not automatically justify the same restrictive treatment for everyone present.

assessment.5. Severity of the measures and chilling: The measures were serious in practice. The applicants were searched in public, some were handcuffed, all were transported away from the protest, and they remained at the station for up to three hours; some were also photographed and fingerprinted, according to their statements (see paragraphs 13-14 and 23). That combination of coercive measures effectively neutralised their participation in the demonstration. Even though the administrative cases against two applicants were later discontinued as time-barred and there was apparently no decision concerning the first applicant, the temporary deprivation of their ability to continue the protest had already occurred (see paragraphs 15-17). The Court has consistently treated such measures as having a substantial deterrent effect on future participation in public debate (see no. 31349/20).

assessment.6. Domestic review and sufficiency of re: The domestic response does not appear to have contained a Convention-compliant balancing exercise. The internal investigation accepted the searches in general terms but did not explain why all applicants had to be removed from the event, and it confirmed procedural unlawfulness in the handling of the detention-related paperwork (see paragraphs 18-21). The criminal investigation into alleged unlawful interference was repeatedly discontinued and reopened and was still pending years later (see paragraphs 22-24). This weakens the Government’s position that the interference was carefully justified by relevant and sufficient reasons at domestic level, which is an important factor under Article 10 (see no. 1162/22).

assessment.7. Overall assessment: The case contains facts that could justify targeted preventive action, especially against demonstrators actually carrying knives, rods or other dangerous items (see paragraphs 8, 12 and 23). But Article 10 requires a close fit between the risk identified and the restrictions imposed. On the facts provided, the police response appears to have been blanket in character, removing all applicants from a peaceful public-interest demonstration without individualized reasons and through a station transfer whose legal basis was defective under domestic law (see paragraphs 14 and 21(i)). In those circumstances, the interference was not shown to be convincingly prescribed by law and, in any event, was disproportionate to the legitimate aims pursued.
